sections.title: Reading Passage 3 — El Nino
sections.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions below. Choose the correct letter A, B, C or D.
sections.passage:
El Nino

The weather phenomenon called El Nino was first recorded in the 1500s when fishermen in South America noticed that near Christmas some years the water was noticeably warmer than others. They named this El Nino, or the infant, as it happened near the celebration of the birth of Christ.

Only in recent years has there been any serious investigations into the causes and results of El Nino. The 1997-1998 El Nino was the first to be studied extensively. Scientists from France, Japan, Korea and Taiwan combined the various readings they had from satellite and surface measurements of wind speeds and water temperatures to make the Tropical Atmosphere Ocean Array. This combined information allowed them to see the overall patterns of an El Nino and helped them predict when one was starting.

Weather patterns rely heavily on the operation of the planetary heat engine. Essentially, this means that because the sun is closest to the equator the seawater in that region is the warmest. The warm water evaporates and forms clouds, which move toward the poles powered by their heat. These atmospheric loops, which move heat from the tropics to the poles, are called connective cells. Without this process the equatorial regions would be hotter than they are and the north and south would be much colder.

The wind in the central Pacific tends to blow from the east. This pushes water from South America towards Australia and Indonesia. As a result, sea levels have been found to be up to 60 centimetres higher in the west. The water that is pushed westward from the South American coast is replaced by colder water, which has a high nutrient level that consequently attracts fish. This makes the waters off Peru and Ecuador good fishing grounds.

An El Nino happens when the winds weaken and sea levels drop. The warmer water moves east and less water evaporates to form clouds. The results of this are twofold. The warmer water in the east reduces the number of fish and the lack of rain causes droughts. This can cause problems such as the forest fires that have plagued Indonesia and Australia in recent years.

As the population has increased the effects of changing weather have had a greater impact. People are living in places, often in areas more likely to be affected by adverse weather, than they ever did before and in increased densities.

Knowing when an El Nino is developing allows people to make plans to lessen its negative effects. The system of buoys and satellites monitoring the Pacific allows scientists to predict the start of the 12 to 18 month El Nino cycle. As a result people can prepare. For example, in North East Brazil during the 1987 El Nino, farmers only got 15% of their normal grain harvest, but in 1992, when the government advised them to plant fast maturing plants, they got 82%.

sections.passage:
How Sled Dogs and Pets Respond When the Clocks Change

A study from the University of Toronto found that sled dogs in Ontario experience disruptions when clocks change for daylight saving time. Published in PLoS One, the research placed movement sensors on sled dogs at Haliburton Forest Wildlife Reserve. After clocks fell back, dogs were active an hour earlier than usual, showing their internal clocks had not adjusted.

Pet dogs of the same breeds — Siberian Huskies and Alaskan Malamutes — showed no such effect, sleeping through the extra hour without restlessness. Dr. Lavania Nagendran was surprised by the difference between working and pet dogs. The research is part of a broader study on behavioural differences between wolves and domestic dogs.

The 2021 study fitted motion trackers onto 25 sled dogs and 29 pet dogs in and near Ontario. Pet owners kept detailed notes about their animals' behavior. Sled dogs, whose schedules were dictated by handlers, found the shift jarring — they were up an hour before handlers appeared the next morning.

Despite initial disruption, sled dogs quickly adapted by the second day. Pet dogs showed no measurable difference in activity levels, possibly because their routines were less regimented. The study suggests working dogs may benefit from gradual transitions when schedules change.

The researchers also noted that sled dogs showed more signs of stress during the transition period, including increased panting and restlessness. This suggests that sudden schedule changes can have physiological effects on animals, not just behavioral ones.

The findings have implications for other working animals, such as farm dogs, zoo animals, and service dogs. If sudden time changes cause stress in sled dogs, similar effects might be seen in other animals whose schedules are tightly controlled by humans.

The study also raises questions about how daylight saving time affects wild animals. While wild animals do not follow human schedules, their behavior is influenced by natural light cycles. Changes in the timing of sunrise and sunset could potentially affect their feeding patterns, migration, and breeding behaviors.

Dr. Nagendran noted that more research is needed to understand the full impact of time changes on animals. She plans to conduct follow-up studies to see if sled dogs show similar disruptions during the spring time change, when clocks move forward rather than back.

sections.passage:
Indian Marriages

Marriage is one of the oldest human institutions and this is as true in Indian culture as anywhere else. In India marriage, called Kanyadana or donating a virgin, is thought of as the greatest sacrifice that a father can make and for the groom as an obligation to perpetuate his bloodline. Many people believe that a marriage is still binding after death.

In early times girls were thought to be ready for marriage after puberty and later even children could be married. Divorce and remarriage were not always possible. By Medieval times marriage was compulsory for girls, who very often married between the ages of eight and nine. Among those able to afford it, polygamy was common and rulers would often have one wife from their own region and other minor wives from other areas. Now, divorce and remarriage is possible and non-Muslim Indian men can only have one wife.

Although there are many regional variations, some features of the Indian wedding ceremony are similar throughout the country. In general weddings are very complicated events and involve long negotiations about dowry payments prior to the event. After this has been decided a day is chosen by asking an astrologer to find a lucky day.

The night before, the bride, her friends and female relatives gather together for a party called a mehendi, where they paint each other's hands and feet with Henna and dance and listen to music. Her guests often give the bride advice about married life and tease her about her future husband. Weddings are traditionally held at the bride's home or in a temple, but parks, hotels and marriage halls are becoming increasingly popular.

The clothing a couple wear on their wedding day varies between regions and ethnic groups. Women most commonly wear a sari. The bride wears a lot of jewelry as this symbolizes the prosperity she will bring to her new family. The groom wears traditional costume or a suit.

The ceremony begins with a mixture of tumeric, sandlewood paste and oils being applied to the couples face and arms. Then they are showered in flowers. After this they perform the rituals that will make them man and wife. First they garland each other and then take seven symbolic steps together representing seven gifts and seven promises.

Finally they say the vows and then they are legally married. The bride's father or guardian takes her hands and puts them in her husband's giving her to him. Now she is no longer a member of her father's family, but a member of her husband's.

After the wedding ceremony, the couple go to the groom's house. The bride should be careful to enter the house right foot first for luck. In the evening the families and their guests celebrate with dancing, music and food.

sections.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions below. Choose the correct letter A, B, C or D.
sections.passage:
Predicting Baby Gender

Old wives tales abound for influencing or predicting the sex of a baby. Parents supposedly should move beds, time ovulation, judge bump shapes, or study swinging wedding rings. A Nature report from September 25, 1997 suggests older husbands might be more reliable predictors of the sex of a child than are old wives.

The difference between the ages of the parents appears to have a small but significant effect on the sex of their first child. Dr. John T. Manning and colleagues from the University of Liverpool discovered this using historical population records from England and Wales. The bigger the parental age difference, the more biased the child sex ratio, with older fathers producing more boys.

Results stem from a noticeable change in marriage and birth patterns around wartime. The team states the proportion of male to female births increases during and shortly after periods of war, with male births rising to about 51.5% around both World Wars. The average age difference between spouses changed in favour of older husbands around those times.

Statistical tests linked the two observations, showing age difference between spouses was strongly correlated with the sex ratio between the years 1911 and 1952. For first-borns, researchers found an excess of daughters when the mother was older than the father and an excess of sons when the father was older than the mother.

But statistics yields only trends, not reasons. It seems natural to increase boy births when males were depleted during wars. Generally there is a small bias towards male births which may compensate for the slightly lower male life-expectancy. However, the mechanisms that cause the bias are a mystery.

Rank and dominance in some animals is related to the sex of offspring. Researchers suggest the bias may result from women preferring to marry older men with higher resources. Hormonal influences of rank and status might also influence early miscarriage or the implant rates of embryos of a particular sex.

The author warns against trading partners for one of appropriate age. The effect is small and noticeable only on the scale of whole populations, not individual cases. The swinging wedding band may turn out to be a more reliable guide.

sections.passage:
The Power of Advertising

Advertising is one of the most powerful forces in modern society. It shapes our desires, influences our purchasing decisions, and even affects how we perceive ourselves and others. The global advertising industry is worth hundreds of billions of dollars, and its influence extends far beyond simple product promotion.

The earliest forms of advertising appeared in ancient civilizations, where merchants would use signs and symbols to attract customers. However, modern advertising as we know it began in the 19th century with the rise of mass media. Newspapers and magazines provided the first platforms for widespread commercial messaging.

The 20th century saw the development of radio and television advertising, which revolutionized the industry. Advertisers could now reach millions of people simultaneously, using sound and moving images to create emotional connections with consumers. The famous 'Mad Men' era of the 1960s saw advertising become an art form, with creative agencies developing sophisticated campaigns that appealed to consumers' desires and aspirations.

Today, digital advertising has transformed the landscape once again. Social media platforms, search engines, and websites collect vast amounts of data about users' behavior, preferences, and demographics. This data allows advertisers to target their messages with unprecedented precision, showing specific ads to specific people at specific times.

Critics argue that advertising creates artificial needs and promotes materialism. They point out that many advertisements use psychological manipulation to make people feel inadequate unless they purchase certain products. Studies have shown that exposure to advertising can increase feelings of anxiety and depression, particularly among young people.

However, supporters of advertising argue that it plays a vital role in the economy. Advertising funds free media content, supports jobs in creative industries, and helps businesses reach customers. Without advertising, many newspapers, television shows, and websites would not be able to operate.

The debate about advertising's impact on society continues. As technology advances and new forms of advertising emerge, the question of how to balance commercial interests with social well-being becomes increasingly important.

sections.title: Reading Passage 2 — Child Obesity
sections.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions below. Choose the correct letter A, B, C or D.
sections.passage:
Child Obesity: A Growing Crisis

Child obesity has become one of the most serious public health challenges of the 21st century. The World Health Organization estimates that the number of overweight or obese children under five years old has increased from 32 million in 1990 to 41 million in 2016. This alarming trend has significant implications for children's health, healthcare systems, and society as a whole.

The causes of child obesity are complex and multifactorial. Changes in dietary patterns, including increased consumption of processed foods, sugary drinks, and fast food, have contributed significantly to the problem. At the same time, physical activity levels have declined as children spend more time watching television, playing video games, and using smartphones and tablets.

Environmental factors also play a role. Many families live in 'food deserts' where fresh, healthy food is difficult to access or afford. Advertising of unhealthy foods targeted at children further exacerbates the problem. Studies have shown that children who watch more television are more likely to consume unhealthy foods and beverages.

The health consequences of child obesity are severe. Obese children are at higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and certain types of cancer. They are also more likely to experience psychological problems, including low self-esteem, depression, and bullying. These health risks often persist into adulthood, creating a significant burden on healthcare systems.

Addressing child obesity requires a comprehensive approach involving families, schools, governments, and the food industry. Schools can promote healthy eating and physical activity through education and policies. Governments can implement regulations on food advertising, improve food labeling, and invest in public health campaigns.

Parents play a crucial role in shaping children's eating habits and activity levels. Research shows that children are more likely to eat healthy foods when their parents model healthy eating behaviors. Family meals, regular physical activity, and limiting screen time are all effective strategies for preventing childhood obesity.

Despite the challenges, there are signs of progress. Some countries have implemented successful interventions, including sugar taxes, restrictions on food advertising to children, and improvements to school meal programs. These efforts demonstrate that childhood obesity can be addressed through coordinated action.

sections.title: Reading Passage 3 — The Rise of Remote Working
sections.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions below. Choose the correct letter A, B, C or D.
sections.passage:
The Rise of Remote Working

The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated a trend that had been slowly building for decades: the shift toward remote working. Before the pandemic, only about 5% of full-time employees in the United States worked from home. By April 2020, that number had surged to over 60%. Even as offices have reopened, remote and hybrid working arrangements have become permanent features of the modern workplace.

The benefits of remote working are well documented. Employees save time and money on commuting, enjoy greater flexibility in managing their work-life balance, and often report higher job satisfaction. Employers benefit from reduced office space costs, access to a wider talent pool, and increased productivity. Studies have shown that remote workers are often more productive than their office-based counterparts, partly because they experience fewer interruptions and can work during their most productive hours.

However, remote working also presents significant challenges. Social isolation is a major concern, as employees miss the informal interactions and sense of community that come from working in an office. Mental health issues, including loneliness and burnout, have increased among remote workers. The blurring of boundaries between work and personal life can make it difficult for employees to 'switch off' and relax.

Communication and collaboration can also be more difficult in a remote environment. While video conferencing tools like Zoom and Microsoft Teams have made it easier to stay connected, they cannot fully replace the spontaneity and richness of face-to-face interactions. Creative brainstorming, mentoring, and building trust with colleagues are all more challenging when working remotely.

The future of work is likely to be hybrid, with employees splitting their time between the office and home. This approach combines the benefits of both arrangements while mitigating their drawbacks. Companies are redesigning their offices to focus on collaboration and social interaction, rather than individual work.

However, the shift to remote and hybrid working has also raised concerns about equity. Not all jobs can be done remotely, creating a divide between knowledge workers who can work from home and essential workers who cannot. There are also concerns about the impact on commercial real estate, as reduced demand for office space affects property values and local businesses that depend on office workers.

Social Media and Mental Health

The relationship between social media use and mental health has become a major area of concern. As platforms like Instagram, TikTok, and Snapchat have become ubiquitous among young people, questions about their psychological impact have intensified.

Research has consistently shown that excessive social media use is associated with higher rates of anxiety, depression, and loneliness. A study by the University of Pennsylvania found that limiting social media use to 30 minutes per day significantly reduced symptoms of depression and loneliness.

Cyberbullying is another serious concern. Unlike traditional bullying, cyberbullying can follow victims home and occur 24 hours a day. Studies have found that victims of cyberbullying are more likely to experience depression, anxiety, and suicidal thoughts.

However, social media also has positive aspects. It can provide a sense of community for people who feel isolated. Social media has also been instrumental in social movements, allowing activists to organize and spread awareness.

The design of social media platforms contributes to their potential for harm. Features like infinite scrolling, push notifications, and algorithmic feeds are designed to maximize user engagement, often at the expense of users' well-being.

Experts recommend a balanced approach to social media use. This includes setting time limits, being mindful of content consumption, and maintaining offline relationships.

The Future of Education

The traditional model of education has remained largely unchanged for over a century. However, technological advances, changing workforce needs, and new research about how people learn are driving a fundamental transformation in education.

One of the most significant changes is the rise of online learning. The COVID-19 pandemic forced schools and universities to adopt remote teaching on an unprecedented scale. While the transition was challenging, it demonstrated that effective learning can happen outside traditional classrooms.

Personalized learning is another emerging trend. Rather than following a one-size-fits-all curriculum, personalized learning uses technology to adapt to each student's pace, interests, and learning style. Artificial intelligence can analyze students' performance and provide customized feedback.

Project-based learning is gaining popularity as an alternative to traditional lecture-based education. Instead of memorizing facts, students work on real-world projects that require critical thinking, collaboration, and creativity.

However, the transformation of education faces significant challenges. Not all students have access to the technology needed for online and personalized learning. The digital divide between wealthy and poor students has become more apparent.

The role of teachers is also evolving. Rather than being the primary source of knowledge, teachers are becoming facilitators and mentors who guide students through their learning journeys.

Despite these challenges, the future of education looks promising. By combining the best of traditional teaching with innovative approaches and technology, we can create learning experiences that are more engaging, effective, and equitable.

Climate Change and Agriculture

Climate change poses a significant threat to global food security. Rising temperatures, changing precipitation patterns, and more frequent extreme weather events are already affecting agricultural production worldwide. The IPCC has warned that without significant adaptation measures, crop yields could decline by up to 25% by 2050.

One of the most direct impacts of climate change on agriculture is the effect of rising temperatures on crop growth. Many staple crops have optimal temperature ranges for growth. When temperatures exceed these ranges, plant development is disrupted, leading to reduced yields.

Water availability is another critical concern. Climate change is altering precipitation patterns, leading to more frequent and severe droughts in some regions and increased flooding in others. Agriculture accounts for approximately 70% of global freshwater withdrawals.

Extreme weather events, such as hurricanes, floods, and droughts, can destroy entire harvests in a matter of days. These events are becoming more frequent and intense due to climate change.

Adaptation strategies are essential for maintaining food production. These include developing drought-resistant crop varieties, improving irrigation efficiency, and adopting sustainable farming practices.

However, adaptation alone is not sufficient. Reducing greenhouse gas emissions from agriculture is also critical. Agriculture is responsible for approximately 10-12% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

International cooperation is essential for addressing the intersection of climate change and agriculture. Developed countries need to support developing nations in adapting to climate change.

sections.passage:
The Growth of Cities

Urbanization is one of the most significant trends of the modern era. In 1950, less than 30% of the world's population lived in cities. Today, that figure has risen to over 56%, and by 2050, it is projected to reach 68%. This massive shift from rural to urban living has profound implications for society, the economy, and the environment.

Cities are engines of economic growth. They concentrate talent, infrastructure, and investment, creating opportunities for innovation and entrepreneurship. Major cities like New York, London, and Tokyo are global financial centers, while cities like Shenzhen and Bangalore have become hubs for technology and innovation. Urban areas generate more than 80% of global GDP, despite covering only about 3% of the Earth's land surface.

However, rapid urbanization also creates significant challenges. Housing affordability is a major concern in many cities, as demand outstrips supply and prices rise beyond the reach of ordinary citizens. Traffic congestion wastes time and increases pollution. In many developing countries, rapid urban growth has led to the expansion of informal settlements or slums, where residents lack access to basic services like clean water, sanitation, and electricity.

Environmental sustainability is another critical issue. Cities consume about 75% of global energy and produce more than 60% of greenhouse gas emissions. Urban sprawl destroys natural habitats and agricultural land. Air pollution in cities poses serious health risks, with the World Health Organization estimating that it causes approximately 4.2 million premature deaths annually.

To address these challenges, many cities are adopting smart city technologies. These include intelligent transportation systems that reduce congestion, energy-efficient buildings that reduce carbon emissions, and digital platforms that improve public services. Singapore, for example, has implemented a comprehensive smart city strategy that uses data analytics and sensors to manage everything from traffic flow to waste collection.

Sustainable urban planning is also essential. This includes creating compact, walkable neighborhoods that reduce the need for cars, investing in public transportation, and preserving green spaces. Copenhagen is often cited as a model for sustainable urban development, with its extensive cycling infrastructure and commitment to becoming carbon neutral by 2025.

The future of cities will depend on our ability to balance economic growth with social equity and environmental sustainability. As the world becomes increasingly urbanized, the decisions we make about city planning and governance will have far-reaching consequences for generations to come.

sections.title: Reading Passage 2 — The Importance of Sleep
sections.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions below. Choose the correct letter A, B, C or D.
sections.passage:
The Importance of Sleep

Sleep is one of the most fundamental biological processes, yet it is often undervalued in modern society. The average adult needs seven to nine hours of sleep per night, but studies show that a significant proportion of the population regularly gets less than this. The consequences of chronic sleep deprivation are far more serious than most people realize.

During sleep, the body performs essential maintenance functions. Growth hormones are released, tissues are repaired, and the immune system is strengthened. The brain also uses sleep to consolidate memories and process information from the day. Research has shown that people who sleep well after learning new information retain it better than those who stay awake.

Lack of sleep has been linked to a wide range of health problems. Chronic sleep deprivation increases the risk of obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and even certain types of cancer. It also weakens the immune system, making people more susceptible to infections. Mental health is also affected, with sleep deprivation being strongly associated with depression and anxiety.

The impact of sleep deprivation on cognitive performance is particularly concerning. Studies have shown that being awake for 24 hours impairs cognitive function to the same extent as being legally drunk. Reaction times slow, decision-making ability declines, and creativity is reduced. This has serious implications for professions that require sustained attention, such as healthcare workers, pilots, and truck drivers.

The modern lifestyle has created numerous obstacles to good sleep. Artificial light, particularly the blue light emitted by smartphones and computers, suppresses the production of melatonin, the hormone that regulates sleep. Caffeine, consumed by billions of people daily, can remain in the system for up to eight hours, disrupting sleep patterns. Shift work, which affects approximately 20% of the workforce, fundamentally disrupts the body's natural circadian rhythm.

Improving sleep quality requires a multifaceted approach. Sleep hygiene practices, such as maintaining a regular sleep schedule, creating a dark and quiet sleep environment, and avoiding screens before bedtime, can significantly improve sleep quality. For those with chronic sleep disorders, medical intervention may be necessary.

The economic cost of sleep deprivation is substantial. A study by the RAND Corporation estimated that sleep deprivation costs the U.S. economy up to $411 billion annually due to reduced productivity and increased healthcare costs. This figure underscores the importance of treating sleep as a public health priority.

sections.title: Reading Passage 3 — The Gig Economy
sections.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions below. Choose the correct letter A, B, C or D.
sections.passage:
The Gig Economy

The gig economy refers to a labor market characterized by the prevalence of short-term contracts or freelance work as opposed to permanent jobs. This type of work arrangement has grown dramatically in recent years, driven by technology platforms like Uber, Airbnb, and TaskRabbit that connect workers with customers.

Proponents of the gig economy argue that it offers unprecedented flexibility. Workers can choose when, where, and how much they work. This is particularly attractive to people who need to balance work with other commitments, such as students, parents, or retirees. The gig economy also provides opportunities for people who might struggle to find traditional employment, including those with disabilities or those living in areas with limited job markets.

However, critics argue that the gig economy creates a precarious workforce with few protections. Gig workers typically do not receive benefits such as health insurance, paid leave, or retirement contributions. They have no job security and can be 'deactivated' from platforms without warning or explanation. The lack of a steady income makes it difficult to plan for the future or obtain loans and mortgages.

The classification of gig workers is a contentious legal issue. Many platforms classify their workers as independent contractors rather than employees, which allows them to avoid providing benefits and protections. However, several courts have ruled that some gig workers should be classified as employees. In 2021, the UK Supreme Court ruled that Uber drivers were 'workers' entitled to minimum wage and holiday pay.

The gig economy also raises questions about labor rights and collective bargaining. Traditional unions are difficult to organize among gig workers because they are dispersed and work independently. New forms of worker organization are emerging, including online communities and app-based cooperatives, but their effectiveness remains to be seen.

Despite these challenges, the gig economy continues to grow. A study by McKinsey estimated that up to 162 million people in the United States and Europe participate in some form of independent work. As the economy evolves, policymakers face the challenge of balancing the flexibility that workers and businesses desire with the protections that workers need.

The future of the gig economy will likely depend on regulatory developments. Some countries have introduced new laws to protect gig workers, while others are still debating the best approach. The outcome of these debates will shape the nature of work for millions of people around the world.

The debate about how to reduce crime is complex. While some advocate longer prison sentences, I believe alternative approaches are more effective.

Proponents of longer sentences argue they deter crime and keep criminals off the streets. If potential offenders know they face severe punishment, they may think twice before committing crimes.

However, research suggests that longer sentences have limited deterrent effect. Many crimes are committed impulsively. Moreover, prisons can become schools for crime, with inmates learning from each other.

Better alternatives include investing in education, addressing poverty, and providing mental health support. Community service and rehabilitation programs have shown success in reducing reoffending.

sections.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions below. Choose the correct letter A, B, C or D.
sections.passage:
The Renewable Energy Revolution

The world is undergoing a profound energy transition. Fossil fuels, which have powered industrial civilization for over two centuries, are gradually being replaced by renewable energy sources. Solar, wind, hydroelectric, and geothermal power are growing at unprecedented rates, driven by falling costs, government policies, and growing concerns about climate change.

Solar energy has experienced the most dramatic cost reductions. The price of solar panels has fallen by more than 99% since 1976, making solar power cheaper than coal and natural gas in many regions. In 2022, solar energy accounted for the largest share of new electricity generation capacity added globally. China, the United States, and India are leading the expansion of solar power.

Wind energy has also grown significantly. Offshore wind farms, which can generate more electricity than onshore installations, are being built in the North Sea, the Atlantic Ocean, and the Pacific Ocean. The largest offshore wind farm, Hornsea 2 in the UK, has a capacity of 1.3 gigawatts, enough to power over 1.3 million homes.

The transition to renewable energy is not without challenges. Solar and wind power are intermittent, meaning they only generate electricity when the sun is shining or the wind is blowing. This requires energy storage solutions, such as batteries, to ensure a reliable supply of electricity. The cost of battery storage has fallen dramatically, but further improvements are needed.

Another challenge is the need for grid infrastructure. Many renewable energy sources are located in remote areas, far from population centers. New transmission lines are needed to bring this electricity to where it is needed. This requires significant investment and can face opposition from local communities.

Despite these challenges, the momentum behind renewable energy is unstoppable. Many countries have set ambitious targets for renewable energy adoption. The European Union aims to generate 45% of its energy from renewable sources by 2030. China, the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases, has pledged to become carbon neutral by 2060.

The economic benefits of renewable energy are also significant. The renewable energy sector employs millions of people worldwide and is creating new industries and jobs. As the technology continues to improve and costs continue to fall, renewable energy is becoming the cheapest form of new electricity generation in most parts of the world.

sections.title: Reading Passage 2 — The Death of Languages
sections.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions below. Choose the correct letter A, B, C or D.
sections.passage:
The Death of Languages

Of the approximately 7,000 languages spoken in the world today, nearly half are endangered. Linguists predict that by the end of this century, up to 90% of the world's languages could become extinct. This loss of linguistic diversity represents not just a cultural tragedy, but also a loss of valuable knowledge about the natural world and human cognition.

Languages die for a variety of reasons. Globalization and the dominance of major languages like English, Mandarin, and Spanish make it economically advantageous for people to learn these languages rather than maintain their native tongues. Urbanization draws people away from rural communities where minority languages are spoken. Government policies that promote a single national language can suppress minority languages.

The death of a language means the loss of a unique way of understanding the world. Each language encodes a distinct set of knowledge, values, and perspectives. Indigenous languages, for example, often contain detailed knowledge about local ecosystems, medicinal plants, and sustainable farming practices that has been accumulated over centuries.

Efforts to preserve endangered languages are underway around the world. Language documentation projects record native speakers using their languages in everyday situations. Language revitalization programs teach endangered languages to new generations of speakers. Technology is also playing a role, with apps and online platforms making it easier for people to learn and use minority languages.

However, these efforts face significant challenges. Many endangered languages have few remaining speakers, and when the last speaker dies, the language is lost forever. Funding for language preservation is often limited, and there is a tension between the desire to preserve languages and the practical need for people to learn major languages for economic advancement.

Some success stories offer hope. The revival of Hebrew, which was once a dead language used only for religious purposes, demonstrates that languages can be brought back to life with sustained effort. The Maori language in New Zealand has seen a resurgence in recent decades, thanks to government support and the establishment of Maori-language schools.

The preservation of linguistic diversity requires a multifaceted approach. Governments need to recognize and protect minority language rights. Communities need to value and use their languages. And technology can help make language learning more accessible and engaging.

sections.title: Reading Passage 3 — Food Security Challenges
sections.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions below. Choose the correct letter A, B, C or D.
sections.passage:
Food Security Challenges

Food security, defined as reliable access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food, remains one of the world's most pressing challenges. Despite significant progress in reducing hunger over the past few decades, approximately 735 million people still face chronic hunger. The COVID-19 pandemic, climate change, and geopolitical conflicts have reversed years of progress and highlighted the fragility of global food systems.

Climate change poses a significant threat to food production. Rising temperatures, changing precipitation patterns, and more frequent extreme weather events are reducing crop yields in many regions. The IPCC has warned that without adaptation, global crop yields could decline by up to 25% by 2050. This is particularly concerning given that the world's population is projected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050.

The global food system is also highly unequal. While some countries produce more food than they consume, others struggle to feed their populations. International trade in agricultural products helps balance supply and demand, but it also creates dependencies and vulnerabilities. The war in Ukraine, for example, disrupted global grain supplies, leading to food price spikes and increased hunger in developing countries.

Technological innovation offers hope for improving food security. Precision agriculture, which uses sensors, drones, and data analytics to optimize farming practices, can increase yields while reducing resource use. Genetic engineering can create crop varieties that are more resistant to pests, diseases, and environmental stresses. Vertical farming and hydroponics can produce food in urban areas, reducing the need for transportation.

However, technology alone cannot solve the problem of food security. Access to food is often limited by poverty, inequality, and conflict. Addressing food security requires not only increasing production but also improving distribution, reducing waste, and addressing the root causes of poverty and conflict.

Food waste is a particularly significant issue. Approximately one-third of all food produced globally is lost or wasted. In developing countries, food is often lost during production and storage due to inadequate infrastructure. In developed countries, food is wasted at the retail and consumer levels. Reducing food waste could significantly improve food security while also reducing the environmental impact of agriculture.

The challenge of feeding the world sustainably requires a fundamental transformation of food systems. This includes adopting more sustainable farming practices, reducing reliance on chemical inputs, promoting plant-based diets, and strengthening local food systems. International cooperation and investment in agricultural research and development are also essential.

sections.passage:
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare

Artificial intelligence is transforming healthcare in ways that were unimaginable just a decade ago. From diagnosing diseases to discovering new drugs, AI is being applied to some of medicine's most challenging problems. The global AI in healthcare market is projected to reach $187 billion by 2030, reflecting the enormous potential of this technology.

One of the most promising applications of AI is in medical imaging. AI algorithms can analyze X-rays, MRIs, and CT scans with accuracy that matches or exceeds that of human radiologists. For example, Google's DeepMind has developed an AI system that can detect over 50 eye diseases from retinal scans with 94% accuracy. This technology can help address the shortage of specialists in many parts of the world.

AI is also being used to accelerate drug discovery. Traditional drug development takes an average of 12 years and costs billions of dollars. AI can analyze vast databases of molecular structures and predict which compounds are most likely to be effective against specific diseases. This has the potential to significantly reduce the time and cost of bringing new drugs to market.

Personalized medicine is another area where AI shows great promise. By analyzing a patient's genetic makeup, medical history, and lifestyle factors, AI can help doctors develop treatment plans tailored to the individual. This approach has shown particular promise in oncology, where AI can help identify the most effective chemotherapy regimen for each patient.

However, the adoption of AI in healthcare also raises significant concerns. Privacy and data security are major issues, as AI systems require access to large amounts of sensitive patient data. There are also concerns about bias in AI algorithms, which may perform differently for different demographic groups. If not carefully addressed, these biases could exacerbate existing health disparities.

The integration of AI into clinical practice also presents challenges. Doctors need training to effectively use AI tools, and there are questions about liability when AI systems make errors. The relationship between doctors and patients could also be affected, as some patients may be uncomfortable with AI playing a role in their care.

Despite these challenges, the potential benefits of AI in healthcare are enormous. As the technology continues to improve and these concerns are addressed, AI has the potential to make healthcare more accurate, accessible, and affordable for people around the world.

sections.passage:
The Impact of Tourism

Tourism is one of the world's largest industries, generating over $8 trillion in revenue annually and supporting approximately 330 million jobs globally. However, the impact of tourism extends far beyond economics. It affects cultures, environments, and communities in both positive and negative ways.

The economic benefits of tourism are well documented. In many developing countries, tourism is a major source of foreign exchange and employment. It can stimulate the development of infrastructure, including airports, roads, and hotels. Tourism also creates opportunities for small businesses, from restaurants and shops to tour guides and handicraft producers.

However, the economic benefits of tourism are not always evenly distributed. Large multinational hotel chains and tour operators often capture most of the revenue, while local communities receive only a small fraction. This phenomenon, known as economic leakage, can limit the positive impact of tourism on local economies.

The environmental impact of tourism is a growing concern. Mass tourism can damage natural habitats, pollute water sources, and contribute to climate change through transportation emissions. Popular destinations like Venice, Barcelona, and Maya Bay in Thailand have struggled with overtourism, which degrades the quality of life for residents and damages the very attractions that draw visitors.

Cultural impacts are complex. Tourism can help preserve cultural heritage by providing economic incentives for the maintenance of historical sites and traditional practices. However, it can also lead to the commodification of culture, where traditions are modified or performed solely for tourist consumption. This can erode the authenticity of cultural practices.

Sustainable tourism aims to minimize negative impacts while maximizing benefits for local communities. This includes promoting responsible travel behavior, supporting locally-owned businesses, and implementing environmental conservation measures. Ecotourism, which focuses on nature-based experiences and environmental education, is one approach to sustainable tourism.

Community-based tourism is another model that seeks to ensure that local people benefit directly from tourism. In this model, communities manage and control tourism activities, ensuring that revenues are used for local development. Examples include community-run lodges in Africa and village homestay programs in Asia.

The challenge for the tourism industry is to find a balance between economic growth and the preservation of natural and cultural resources. This requires cooperation between governments, businesses, and local communities to develop and implement sustainable tourism strategies.

Water Scarcity: A Global Crisis

Water is essential for life, yet billions of people around the world lack access to clean, safe drinking water. According to the United Nations, approximately 2.2 billion people do not have safely managed drinking water services. This water crisis has profound implications for health, economic development, and social stability.

Water scarcity is driven by a combination of factors. Population growth increases demand for water, while climate change alters precipitation patterns and reduces water availability in many regions. Pollution from agricultural runoff, industrial waste, and untreated sewage contaminates water sources. Inefficient water use in agriculture, which accounts for approximately 70% of global freshwater withdrawals, exacerbates the problem.

The consequences of water scarcity are severe. Lack of access to clean water leads to waterborne diseases such as cholera, typhoid, and dysentery, which kill hundreds of thousands of people each year. Children are particularly vulnerable, with diarrhea being the second leading cause of death in children under five.

Water scarcity also affects economic development. In many developing countries, women and girls spend hours each day collecting water, limiting their ability to attend school or participate in the workforce. Industries that depend on water, such as agriculture, manufacturing, and energy production, are also affected.

Addressing water scarcity requires a multifaceted approach. Improving water infrastructure, including pipes, treatment plants, and storage facilities, can reduce water loss and improve access. Water-efficient technologies, such as drip irrigation and water recycling, can reduce consumption. Protecting and restoring natural ecosystems, such as wetlands and forests, can help maintain water quality and availability.

Desalination, the process of removing salt from seawater, is increasingly being used to provide fresh water in coastal areas. While desalination technology has improved significantly, it remains energy-intensive and expensive. However, as water scarcity becomes more severe, desalination is becoming a more viable option for many countries.

International cooperation is essential for addressing water scarcity. Many of the world's major rivers and aquifers cross national boundaries, requiring agreements on water sharing and management. The United Nations has recognized access to clean water as a human right, and sustainable development goals include targets for universal access to safe drinking water by 2030.

The water crisis is a complex challenge that requires action at all levels, from individual conservation efforts to international policy. By investing in infrastructure, adopting efficient technologies, and protecting natural resources, we can work toward a future where everyone has access to the clean water they need.

sections.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions below. Choose the correct letter A, B, C or D.
sections.passage:
Public Health in the 21st Century

Public health has undergone a dramatic transformation over the past century. Infectious diseases, which were once the leading cause of death, have been largely controlled through vaccination, sanitation, and antibiotics. Today, the primary health challenges in developed countries are chronic diseases such as heart disease, diabetes, and cancer. However, the COVID-19 pandemic demonstrated that infectious diseases remain a significant threat.

The rise of chronic diseases is closely linked to lifestyle factors. Poor diet, lack of physical activity, smoking, and excessive alcohol consumption are the main drivers of these conditions. Obesity, which has reached epidemic proportions in many countries, is a major risk factor for numerous chronic diseases. The World Health Organization estimates that obesity-related conditions cost the global economy over $2 trillion annually.

Mental health has also emerged as a critical public health concern. Depression is now the leading cause of disability worldwide, affecting more than 260 million people. The stigma surrounding mental illness has decreased in recent years, but access to mental health services remains limited in many countries. The economic cost of mental health conditions is estimated at $1 trillion per year in lost productivity.

Antimicrobial resistance is another growing threat. The overuse and misuse of antibiotics has led to the emergence of drug-resistant bacteria, making infections harder to treat. The WHO has warned that without action, antimicrobial resistance could cause 10 million deaths annually by 2050, surpassing cancer as a cause of death.

Climate change poses additional public health challenges. Rising temperatures increase the spread of vector-borne diseases like malaria and dengue fever. Air pollution, which is exacerbated by climate change, causes approximately 7 million premature deaths annually. Extreme weather events, such as heatwaves and floods, directly threaten human health and safety.

Addressing these challenges requires a comprehensive approach that includes prevention, early detection, and treatment. Governments must invest in public health infrastructure, promote healthy lifestyles, and address the social determinants of health, such as poverty, education, and housing. International cooperation is also essential, as health threats do not respect national boundaries.

sections.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions below. Choose the correct letter A, B, C or D.
sections.passage:
The Digital Economy

The digital economy has transformed the way businesses operate and consumers interact with goods and services. E-commerce, which was once a novelty, now accounts for a significant portion of retail sales worldwide. In 2023, global e-commerce sales exceeded $5.7 trillion, and this figure is projected to grow by 56% over the next few years.

The rise of digital platforms has created new business models and disrupted traditional industries. Companies like Amazon, Alibaba, and Shopify have made it possible for anyone to start an online business with minimal capital. The gig economy, facilitated by platforms like Uber and DoorDash, has created flexible employment opportunities for millions of people.

Digital payments have also transformed commerce. Mobile payment systems like Apple Pay, Google Pay, and various national systems have made cashless transactions the norm in many countries. In China, mobile payments accounted for over 80% of all transactions in 2022. This shift has reduced the cost of handling cash and increased financial inclusion.

However, the digital economy also presents challenges. The digital divide between those who have access to technology and those who do not remains significant. According to the International Telecommunication Union, approximately 2.7 billion people still do not use the internet. This divide can exacerbate existing inequalities in education, healthcare, and economic opportunity.

Data privacy and security are major concerns. The collection and use of personal data by technology companies has raised questions about individual privacy rights. High-profile data breaches have exposed the personal information of millions of users. Governments around the world are implementing data protection regulations, such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

The impact of artificial intelligence on employment is another concern. While AI has the potential to create new jobs and increase productivity, it also threatens to automate many existing roles. A study by McKinsey estimates that up to 30% of work activities could be automated by 2030. This could lead to significant job displacement, particularly in manufacturing, transportation, and customer service.

Despite these challenges, the digital economy offers enormous opportunities for innovation, efficiency, and inclusion. Governments, businesses, and individuals must work together to ensure that the benefits of digitalization are shared broadly and that the risks are managed effectively.

sections.title: Reading Passage 3 — Biodiversity Loss
sections.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions below. Choose the correct letter A, B, C or D.
sections.passage:
Biodiversity Loss: A Silent Crisis

Biodiversity, the variety of life on Earth, is declining at an unprecedented rate. Scientists estimate that species are going extinct at 1,000 times the natural background rate. The Living Planet Report 2022 found that wildlife populations have declined by an average of 69% since 1970. This loss of biodiversity has profound implications for ecosystems, food security, and human well-being.

The main drivers of biodiversity loss are habitat destruction, overexploitation, pollution, invasive species, and climate change. Deforestation, which destroys the habitats of countless species, is a major contributor. The Amazon rainforest, which is home to approximately 10% of all species on Earth, has lost about 17% of its forest cover in the past 50 years.

Overexploitation of species through hunting, fishing, and harvesting is another significant driver. Overfishing has depleted fish stocks in many parts of the world. The Food and Agriculture Organization estimates that approximately 34% of global fish stocks are overfished. This not only threatens marine ecosystems but also the food security of communities that depend on fishing.

Pollution, including plastic waste, chemical runoff, and air pollution, also contributes to biodiversity loss. Plastic pollution in the oceans has reached crisis levels, with an estimated 8 million tons of plastic entering the oceans each year. This plastic harms marine life through ingestion and entanglement.

Invasive species, introduced through trade and travel, can devastate native ecosystems. These species often have no natural predators in their new environments, allowing them to spread rapidly and outcompete native species. Examples include the Asian carp in North American waterways and the cane toad in Australia.

Climate change is increasingly recognized as a major threat to biodiversity. Rising temperatures are forcing species to migrate to cooler areas, disrupting ecosystems. Coral reefs, which support approximately 25% of all marine species, are particularly vulnerable to warming oceans. The Great Barrier Reef has experienced several mass bleaching events in recent years.

Conservation efforts are underway around the world. Protected areas, which now cover approximately 17% of the Earth's land surface, help preserve habitats and species. Breeding programs for endangered species, such as the giant panda and the California condor, have shown success. However, these efforts need to be scaled up significantly to address the magnitude of the crisis.

sections.title: Writing
sections.prompt:
Some of the methods used in advertising are unethical and unacceptable in today's society.

To what extent do you agree with this view?

Write at least 250 words.
sections.sample_answer:
Advertising is an omnipresent feature of modern life, and I strongly agree that many advertising methods used today are unethical and unacceptable.

Firstly, advertising is increasingly intrusive. Advertisements appear on television, the internet, social media, and even on mobile phones via SMS. This constant bombardment leaves consumers with little choice but to be exposed to commercial messages, which many find annoying and disrespectful of their personal space.

Secondly, advertising often encourages people to buy products they neither need nor can afford. This is particularly harmful when targeted at children and young people, who may pressure their parents into making unnecessary purchases. The rise of influencer marketing has made this problem worse, as young people often cannot distinguish between genuine recommendations and paid promotions.

Furthermore, some industries continue to advertise harmful products. While tobacco advertising has been banned in many countries, alcohol advertising remains largely unrestricted despite its potential to encourage excessive consumption and underage drinking.

In conclusion, the unethical methods used in advertising — from intrusive techniques to targeting vulnerable groups — are unacceptable in today's society. Stronger regulations are needed to protect consumers from these practices.

The New Space Race

The 21st century has witnessed a remarkable transformation in space exploration. While the 20th century was dominated by government agencies like NASA and the Soviet space program, the new era is increasingly driven by private companies. SpaceX, Blue Origin, and Virgin Galactic are leading this commercial revolution, fundamentally changing how humanity approaches space.

SpaceX, founded by Elon Musk in 2002, has achieved several historic milestones. In 2020, it became the first private company to send astronauts to the International Space Station. The company's reusable rocket technology has dramatically reduced the cost of space travel. A Falcon 9 launch now costs approximately $62 million, compared to $1.5 billion for the Space Shuttle.

The ultimate goal of many private space companies is to make humanity a multi-planetary species. SpaceX's Starship rocket is designed to carry up to 100 passengers to Mars. The company plans to establish a permanent human settlement on Mars by 2050. However, the challenges are immense. The journey to Mars takes approximately seven months, and astronauts would face radiation exposure, muscle atrophy, and psychological isolation.

Space tourism is another growing sector. Companies like Virgin Galactic and Blue Origin offer suborbital flights to wealthy customers. In July 2021, Richard Branson flew to the edge of space aboard Virgin Galactic's SpaceShipTwo. Just nine days later, Jeff Bezos flew on Blue Origin's New Shepard rocket.

The scientific benefits of space exploration are well documented. Satellites help us monitor climate change, predict natural disasters, and improve telecommunications. The International Space Station has been a laboratory for experiments that could not be conducted on Earth.

Critics argue that the billions spent on space exploration could be better used to solve problems on Earth. However, proponents counter that space technology has led to numerous innovations that benefit everyday life, from memory foam to water purification systems.

sections.passage:
The Psychology of Happiness

What makes people happy? This question has fascinated philosophers for centuries, but it is only in recent decades that psychologists have begun to study happiness scientifically. The field of positive psychology, which emerged in the late 1990s, has produced fascinating insights into the nature of happiness and well-being.

Research has consistently shown that money does buy happiness, but only up to a point. A landmark study by Daniel Kahneman and Angus Deaton found that emotional well-being increases with income up to about $75,000 per year, after which it plateaus. This suggests that while financial security is important for happiness, excessive wealth does not necessarily lead to greater well-being.

Relationships are perhaps the strongest predictor of happiness. The Harvard Study of Adult Development, which has tracked participants for over 80 years, found that the quality of relationships is the single most important factor in determining happiness and longevity. People with strong social connections are happier, healthier, and live longer than those who are isolated.

Gratitude is another powerful predictor of happiness. Research by Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough found that people who regularly practice gratitude — by keeping a gratitude journal, for example — experience higher levels of positive emotions, feel more alive, and are more helpful to others. Gratitude shifts focus from what is lacking to what is present.

Physical exercise is also strongly linked to happiness. Studies have shown that regular exercise can be as effective as antidepressant medication in treating mild to moderate depression. Exercise releases endorphins, reduces stress hormones, and improves sleep quality.

However, the pursuit of happiness can sometimes be counterproductive. Research by Iris Mauss found that the more people value happiness, the lonelier they feel. This paradox suggests that happiness is best achieved indirectly, as a byproduct of meaningful activities and relationships, rather than as a goal in itself.

Mindfulness and meditation have also been shown to increase happiness. Regular meditation practice can reduce stress, improve emotional regulation, and increase feelings of well-being. The growing popularity of mindfulness apps and meditation retreats reflects the increasing recognition of these benefits.

sections.passage:
The Fashion Industry's Environmental Impact

The fashion industry is one of the most polluting industries in the world. It accounts for approximately 10% of global carbon emissions and is the second-largest consumer of water. The production of a single cotton t-shirt requires about 2,700 liters of water — enough for one person to drink for 2.5 years.

Fast fashion, which refers to the rapid production of cheap, trendy clothing, has accelerated the industry's environmental impact. Brands like Zara and H&M produce new collections every few weeks, encouraging consumers to buy more and discard clothing quickly. The average consumer now buys 60% more clothing than they did 15 years ago, but keeps each item for half as long.

Textile waste is a growing problem. In the United States alone, approximately 11 million tons of textile waste end up in landfills each year. Synthetic fabrics, which are made from petroleum, can take hundreds of years to decompose. Even natural fibers like cotton release methane, a potent greenhouse gas, as they break down in landfills.

The production of clothing also contributes to water pollution. The dyeing process uses toxic chemicals that are often discharged into rivers and streams. The Citarum River in Indonesia, which supplies water to over 30 million people, is one of the most polluted rivers in the world due to textile manufacturing.

Sustainable fashion is emerging as an alternative to the fast fashion model. This includes using organic and recycled materials, reducing waste through better design, and promoting circular economy principles where clothing is reused, repaired, and recycled. Brands like Patagonia and Eileen Fisher have pioneered sustainable practices.

Consumer behavior is also changing. The secondhand clothing market is growing rapidly, with platforms like ThredUp and Poshmark making it easier to buy and sell used clothing. Rental services for special occasion clothing are also gaining popularity.

However, the transition to sustainable fashion faces challenges. Sustainable clothing is often more expensive than fast fashion, making it less accessible to lower-income consumers. Additionally, the infrastructure for recycling clothing is still limited in many countries.

The fashion industry must fundamentally change its practices to address its environmental impact. This requires collaboration between brands, consumers, and governments to create a more sustainable and circular fashion system.

sections.title: Writing
sections.prompt:
Government investment in the arts, such as music and theatre, is a waste of money. Governments must invest this money in public services instead.

To what extent do you agree with this statement?

Write at least 250 words.
sections.sample_answer:
The question of whether government funding should prioritize public services over the arts is a contentious issue. While I understand the argument for investing in essential services, I believe that the arts also deserve public funding.

Those who oppose arts funding argue that healthcare, education, and infrastructure should take precedence. These services directly affect people's quality of life, and underfunding them can have serious consequences. For example, inadequate healthcare funding leads to longer waiting times and poorer outcomes for patients.

However, the arts play a vital role in society that should not be underestimated. Museums, theaters, and galleries enrich cultural life and attract tourism, generating economic benefits. Moreover, arts education develops creativity and critical thinking skills that are valuable in the modern workforce.

In conclusion, while public services should certainly be well-funded, this should not come at the complete expense of the arts. A balanced approach that invests in both would benefit society as a whole.

sections.title: Reading Passage 1 — Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
sections.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions below. Choose the correct letter A, B, C or D.
sections.passage:
Ethics of Artificial Intelligence

As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into society, ethical concerns about its development and use have intensified. From autonomous vehicles to facial recognition systems, AI technologies raise fundamental questions about privacy, bias, accountability, and the nature of human decision-making.

One of the most pressing ethical concerns is algorithmic bias. AI systems learn from data, and if that data reflects existing social biases, the AI will perpetuate and even amplify those biases. For example, studies have shown that facial recognition systems are significantly less accurate at identifying people with darker skin tones. This has serious implications for law enforcement and security applications.

Privacy is another major concern. AI-powered surveillance systems can track individuals' movements, analyze their behavior, and predict their actions. In China, a social credit system uses AI to monitor citizens and assign them scores based on their behavior. While proponents argue this improves social order, critics say it creates a surveillance state that violates fundamental rights.

The use of AI in autonomous weapons raises perhaps the most serious ethical questions. Lethal autonomous weapons systems, sometimes called 'killer robots,' can select and engage targets without human intervention. The Campaign to Stop Killer Robots, supported by numerous Nobel laureates and AI researchers, calls for a ban on these systems.

Accountability is another challenge. When an AI system makes a mistake, who is responsible? If an autonomous vehicle causes an accident, is the manufacturer, the programmer, or the owner liable? Current legal frameworks are not equipped to handle these questions.

The impact of AI on employment also raises ethical concerns. While AI has the potential to create new jobs, it also threatens to automate many existing roles. This could lead to significant job displacement and exacerbate income inequality.

Despite these concerns, many argue that the benefits of AI outweigh the risks. AI has the potential to revolutionize healthcare, education, and scientific research. The challenge is to develop AI in a way that maximizes its benefits while minimizing its risks. This requires collaboration between technologists, ethicists, policymakers, and the public.

sections.title: Reading Passage 2 — Ocean Conservation
sections.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions below. Choose the correct letter A, B, C or D.
sections.passage:
Ocean Conservation: Protecting Our Blue Planet

Oceans cover approximately 71% of the Earth's surface and contain 97% of the planet's water. They regulate the climate, produce oxygen, and provide food for billions of people. However, human activities are threatening ocean health at an unprecedented rate.

Overfishing is one of the most serious threats to ocean ecosystems. The Food and Agriculture Organization estimates that approximately 34% of global fish stocks are overfished, meaning they are being harvested faster than they can reproduce. This has devastating consequences for marine ecosystems and the communities that depend on fishing for food and livelihoods.

Plastic pollution is another critical issue. An estimated 8 million tons of plastic enter the oceans each year, harming marine life through ingestion and entanglement. The Great Pacific Garbage Patch, a massive collection of floating plastic debris, covers an area approximately twice the size of Texas. Microplastics, tiny particles of plastic less than 5mm in size, have been found in the deepest ocean trenches and in the tissues of marine animals.

Ocean acidification, caused by the absorption of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, is threatening marine ecosystems. The oceans have become approximately 30% more acidic since the Industrial Revolution. This increased acidity makes it harder for shellfish and coral to build their shells and skeletons, threatening the entire marine food chain.

Coral reefs, which support approximately 25% of all marine species, are particularly vulnerable to climate change. Rising ocean temperatures cause coral bleaching, a phenomenon where corals expel the algae that give them color and nutrition. The Great Barrier Reef has experienced several mass bleaching events in recent years.

Marine protected areas (MPAs) are one tool for ocean conservation. These areas restrict human activities like fishing and mining to protect marine ecosystems. Currently, approximately 8% of the ocean is covered by MPAs, but scientists recommend protecting at least 30% by 2030.

Sustainable fishing practices are also essential. This includes setting catch limits based on scientific data, reducing bycatch (the unintentional capture of non-target species), and eliminating harmful fishing practices like bottom trawling.

The health of the oceans is essential for human survival. Protecting them requires global cooperation and a commitment to sustainable practices.

sections.title: Reading Passage 3 — The Evolution of Remote Work
sections.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions below. Choose the correct letter A, B, C or D.
sections.passage:
The Evolution of Remote Work

The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated a trend that had been slowly building for decades: the shift toward remote working. Before the pandemic, only about 5% of full-time employees in the United States worked from home. By April 2020, that number had surged to over 60%. Even as offices have reopened, remote and hybrid working arrangements have become permanent features of the modern workplace.

The benefits of remote working are well documented. Employees save time and money on commuting, enjoy greater flexibility in managing their work-life balance, and often report higher job satisfaction. Employers benefit from reduced office space costs, access to a wider talent pool, and increased productivity.

However, remote working also presents significant challenges. Social isolation is a major concern, as employees miss the informal interactions and sense of community that come from working in an office. Mental health issues, including loneliness and burnout, have increased among remote workers.

Communication and collaboration can also be more difficult in a remote environment. While video conferencing tools like Zoom and Microsoft Teams have made it easier to stay connected, they cannot fully replace the spontaneity and richness of face-to-face interactions.

The future of work is likely to be hybrid, with employees splitting their time between the office and home. This approach combines the benefits of both arrangements while mitigating their drawbacks. Companies are redesigning their offices to focus on collaboration and social interaction, rather than individual work.

However, the shift to remote and hybrid working has also raised concerns about equity. Not all jobs can be done remotely, creating a divide between knowledge workers who can work from home and essential workers who cannot.

Despite these challenges, the trend toward remote work appears irreversible. Companies that embrace this change and develop effective remote work policies will be better positioned to attract and retain talent in the competitive job market.

sections.title: Writing
sections.prompt:
The graph below shows the number of tourists visiting three different countries between 2000 and 2020.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.
sections.sample_answer:
The line graph illustrates the number of tourists visiting three countries over a twenty-year period from 2000 to 2020.

Overall, all three countries experienced an increase in tourist numbers, with Country A showing the most dramatic growth. In 2000, Country A received approximately 10 million tourists, which rose steadily to around 45 million by 2020. Country B started at 20 million and climbed to about 35 million. Country C had the most stable growth, rising from 15 million to 25 million over the same period.

In conclusion, Country A emerged as the most popular destination by 2020, having overtaken both other countries during the period shown.
